A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Scene Language research. Their complete main texts and appendices, including equations, tables, figures, prompts, and generated programs, support reliable comparison despite substantial reformatting and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports original scene-generation and editing results, including a 103-participant user study over nine prompts and counting accuracy in Table 4.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds generic-prompt comparisons, quantitative 4D and image-conditioned evaluations, component ablations, and failure cases.

M1.justification: The program-word-embedding representation, recursive execution, LM-based inference, textual inversion, and renderer procedures remain substantively unchanged. New editing demonstrations and ablated configurations test the existing method; they do not establish a revised proposed algorithm.

E1.justification: v2 adds eight generic semantic and spatial-relation prompts alongside the nine numeric prompts (Table 3 and Figure 10). It also demonstrates temporal-direction editing of a 4D scene and entity-targeted image-guided editing (Figures 12 and 8), extending the actual evaluation beyond v1's demonstrated scenarios.

E2.justification: v2 introduces 4D-fy as an evaluated comparator for 4D generation. Figure 13(a) also compares GraphDreamer and MVDream against the proposed editing method through scene regeneration; v1 evaluated these methods for generation but excluded them from its editing comparison.

E3.justification: Beyond v1's user preferences, counting accuracy, and qualitative comparisons, v2 adds CLIP evaluation over 120 viewpoints, 4D dynamic-degree evaluation using RAFT, and LPIPS over three image-conditioned scenes with 20 viewpoints each. It also introduces explicit-motion prompt controls and a Llama 3.3 backbone comparison.

E4.justification: Appendix D.4 and Figure 13 introduce No-P, No-W, and No-P-No-W editing ablations, program-removal generation analysis, and a backbone comparison. Appendix D.2 tests whether motion-explicit prompts improve 4D-fy, while Appendix E and Figure 15 add prompt-sensitivity and repeated image-parsing failure analyses.

E5.justification: v2 explicitly identifies Table 3's standard deviations as variation across scenes and newly documents repeated inference samples in Figure 15, including three image parses. v1 already reported standard deviations and 103 participants; no increase in that participant count or new benchmark seed counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests is established.

E6.justification: The original nine-prompt preference and counting results are retained, but Tables 3, 4, and 6 add substantial results. Newly reported 4D scores are CLIP 0.341/dynamic degree 5.9% for ours versus 0.352/0.2% for 4D-fy; image-generation LPIPS is 0.681 versus GraphDreamer's 0.811. Generic-prompt CLIP ties MVDream at the reported 0.328. New ablation, editing, and failure outcomes also appear.

T1.justification: The representation definitions, Gaussian-transformation assumptions and derivation, and SDS/textual-inversion objectives retain their mathematical substance. v2 makes the existing rendering operator explicit in the SDS loss and consolidates the DSL specification; these are notation and specification clarifications rather than new theoretical results or changed mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: The abstract and four listed contributions retain their central meaning. However, the conclusion drops v1's general comparative assertion that its 3D and 4D scenes have significantly higher fidelity than existing methods, retaining a claim of high fidelity without that broad comparison.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive limitations concerning prompt sensitivity, variable image parsing, diffusion-model biases, and coupled shape/texture changes during embedding edits. It also interprets the new 4D comparison as a tradeoff: 4D-fy has higher CLIP alignment, whereas Scene Language produces more motion. Appendix D.4 adds interpretations of the separate roles of programs and words.

D1.justification: Appendix C.1 newly reports hardware and stage runtimes, including approximately 30 minutes per object for SDS rendering. Appendix C.4.2 specifies the evaluation OpenCLIP variant, and Mitsuba's unused differentiability is clarified. Existing prompt templates and textual-inversion settings are retained; the additional disclosures do not demonstrate changes to those experiments.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting its new comparisons and metrics, including 4D-fy, VBench, RAFT, LPIPS, and Krizhevsky (2014), while removing the Instant-NGP reference. The three-part related-work organization and positioning against program, graph, and latent representations remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The six application subsections become two experiment sections organized around text and image prompting. The appendices are extensively reorganized: DSL and renderer details are combined, prompts and responses are grouped together, and existing 4D explanations and discriminative-information discussion move into extended results. Much underlying prose remains recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 adopts a two-column layout, moves the teaser onto the first page, consolidates three DSL tables, expands quantitative displays, and adds comparison, ablation, editing, and failure panels. v1's editing Figure 5 is distributed across Figures 7 and 11. The staircase annotation changes from radius 4.0 to 1.0, matching code already present in v1's appendix.

improvement.justification: The component ablations, motion-prompt controls, broader evaluation, and concrete failure discussion strengthen empirical support and clarify applicability beyond v1. The gains are limited by small qualitative analyses and reporting inconsistencies: Table 3's new generic preference entries total 103.01 despite being labeled percentages, and Appendix C.4.1 still describes only nine study scenes. Overall, the added scrutiny and transparency provide a modest net improvement.
